claims.claim: The books tell the story by hopping between a large repertory company of viewpoint characters spread across Westeros, most of them afraid for their lives.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: hopping about from person to person across the wide geography

claims.claim: Martin kills off central characters who are richly imagined, three-dimensional portraits, which most writers could not bear to lose.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: richly imagined, textured, three-dimensional portraits of central characters

claims.claim: Narrative momentum slows in books four and five, which become leisurely and expansive with overlapping, simultaneous storylines.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: the narrative momentum of the series has slowed

claims.claim: The appeal rests on the depth, texture and thoroughness of the imagined world and the range of imaginative sympathy across a large cast.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: depth and texture and profoundly satisfying thoroughness

claims.claim: The Bran defenestration lands harder in the book than on screen because Bran has already been established as a viewpoint character.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: even more of an impact, perhaps

claims.claim: Lanchester's 4,617-word essay contains no verdict on Martin's diction, sentence rhythm or dialogue; its praise is entirely structural (unpredictability, instability, the seasons as economic metaphor), and the LRB now serves the full text without a paywall.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013

claims.claim: Each chapter is narrated by a different character, so the reader's view of any character is partial, biased or wrong and must be revised as the tale evolves.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: each chapter is narrated by a different character

claims.claim: The fragmented viewpoint storytelling mirrors the theme of power fragmenting societies and individuals.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: This fragmentation in the storytelling nicely mirrors Martin’s larger theme

claims.claim: Martin replaces standard English with compound coinages such as 'sellsword' for mercenary and 'holdfast' for fort.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the compound coinages that replace standard English

claims.claim: The diction and the spellings of names are ingeniously quasi-medieval.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: ingeniously quasi-medieval diction and spellings of names

claims.claim: Period nouns (destriers, palfreys, vair, samite) give a strong sense of the concrete reality of the world and cannot be rendered on screen.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the perfumed language—the horses called destriers and palfreys

claims.claim: The narrative alternates distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus with exotic 'oriental' locales, bearing traces of Scott, Conan Doyle and Costain boys' adventure stories.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus alternating with exotic “oriental” locales

claims.claim: Tyrion's speech sets 'magnificent' destriers beside 'shit', a pointed mock-medieval deflation of romance that asks the reader to see beyond glitter to gore.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: The juxtaposition of “magnificent” and “shit” is pointed

claims.claim: The three-walled description of Qarth (animals, war, sex) reads as a sly reference to the series' own layered decor.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: a sly reference to the series itself

claims.claim: The view of court power is grimly unsentimental and Tacitean, with a tart Thucydidean appreciation of political corruption breeding narrative corruption.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: grimly unsentimental, rather Tacitean view

claims.claim: Eastern cultures are rendered with Herodotean gusto (horse-worshipping Dothraki, quasi-Assyrian city-states, Venetian Braavos).
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: renders the Eastern cultures in particular with Herodotean gusto

claims.claim: The fornication is unsentimental but has a certain imaginative élan (the purple-bearded drunk lapping wine off a wench's breasts).
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: unsentimental fornication that is not without a certain imaginative élan

claims.claim: Brutal, irreversible consequences for characters' actions are part of the epic's distinctive tone and feel more 'literary' than any television series.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: brutal, irreversible real-life consequences

claims.claim: Abandoning the core characters for new ones in the fourth book was a serious misstep; the reviewer took a month because he did not care about the strangers.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: I simply didn’t care about these strangers

claims.claim: Cersei's sword-versus-moonblood speech is an arresting echo of the Greek notion that childbirth is for women what war is for men; Martin carries argument in character monologue.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: an arresting echo of the Greek notion

claims.claim: The theological preoccupations do not raise the books to Lord of the Rings' level of parable; the appeal is thematic ambition plus richly satisfying details.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: richly satisfying details

claims.claim: Each chapter is narrated in the third person from one character's point of view; eight major viewpoint characters in book one grew to seventeen by A Feast for Crows.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: Each chapter is narrated in the third person

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a 'gardener' who has a rough destination but improvises, in contrast to Tolkien the 'architect' who built languages and histories first.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: he has a rough idea where he’s going but improvises

claims.claim: Martin fleshes out only as much world as the story needs and has invented only seven words of High Valyrian.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: I’ve invented seven words of High Valyrian

claims.claim: Martin drew on the Wars of the Roses rather than mythology, used relatively little magic, and the result felt dangerous, lusty and real.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: it felt dangerous, lusty, and real

claims.claim: Martin suspects he rewrites too much, ripping one Tyrion chapter out and putting it back for ten years, even trying it as a dream sequence.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: Maybe I’m rewriting too much

claims.claim: Aligning the chronologies of seventeen viewpoint characters' travel times across two books bedevils the writing.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: The ‘Dance’ timeline alone is a bitch and a half

claims.claim: Fans catch small continuity slips (a horse that changes sex, eyes green then blue) because every line is analysed.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: People are analyzing every goddam line in these books

claims.claim: The narrative is intricate and racy, practically custom-built for HBO ('The Sopranos in Middle-earth').
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: the book’s intricate, racy narrative

claims.claim: Martin's taste for pageantry and colour (his medieval miniature dioramas) carries into the fiction.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: I like the pageantry and the color

claims.claim: More than a thousand named characters exist by a superfan's count; Martin quotes Tolkien that the tale grew in the telling.
claims.source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
claims.quote: The tale grew in the telling

claims.claim: The prose is shoddy and inconsistent while also being heavily repetitive.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: His prose is shoddy and inconsistent

claims.claim: Readers themselves mock recurring formulas such as 'as useless as nipples on a breastplate'.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: as useless as nipples on a breastplate

claims.claim: Dialogue is grandiose and swear-ridden but has little substance; the Darkstar 'I am of the night' exchange is cringeworthy and its symbolism incomprehensible.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: behind the ostentatious fluff, there’s little substance

claims.claim: Martin is obsessed with expendable details (every feast dish, a character's gynecomastia), which bloats the books.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: completely obsessed with expendable details

claims.claim: The Oberyn–Mountain duel has no symbolism, metaphor or manipulated time and no build-up to catharsis, only the shock of a hero dying; the stableboy's death is sensational violence.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: No literary devices such as symbolism, metaphors, even the fucking pacing

claims.claim: The duel's repeated 'You raped her. You murdered her. You killed her children' refrain is reproduced at length as evidence of flat, unbuilt violence.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)

claims.claim: The summary verdict is that the prose is not poetic, the dialogue can be childish and the story convoluted.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: His prose is not poetic, his dialogue can be childish

claims.claim: Because viewpoint characters must lack foresight of their fate, POV status itself predicts tribulation and makes the 'anyone can die' twists predictable.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: readers already expect their POV characters to experience tribulation

claims.claim: Jaime's 'arc' is perception development: Martin warps the reader's view via backstory rather than changing the character.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: What passes off as “character development” is actually “perception development.”

claims.claim: Characters are one-dimensional, focused on singular interests, and sortable into a 'Hall of Tropes' (Patriarch, Ideal Hero, Ax-Crazy).
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: one-dimensional and comically focused on singular interests

claims.claim: Cersei may be the only viewpoint character who is completely unsympathetic; her POV chapters repeatedly tell rather than show that she would fare better as a man.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011
claims.quote: We are told repeatedly in her POV chapters

claims.claim: Dany reads as a white saviour whose errors cost her little, and Drogo as a Noble Savage; the essay is about characterization and politics, not sentence craft.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011
claims.quote: a feminist icon she ain’t

claims.claim: The books are great and hold a mirror to our world but suffer from the faults they try to expose.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011
claims.quote: These books are great

claims.claim: For a thousand pages almost nothing happens and then there are cliffhangers; the book is too long and painfully slow.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: It’s too long. It’s painfully slow.

claims.claim: The book feels unedited; a bold editor with a red pen could have cut it by nearly half.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: A good edit would have slashed this book by nearly half

claims.claim: Single-chapter viewpoint characters feel hobbled by their brevity; Kain wants established characters, not new ones.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: so hobbled by their brevity

claims.claim: The book oscillates between excellent Northern chapters and the most boring moments in any fantasy series, with Dany's chapters actively hurting the books.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: It oscillates wildly between excellent chapters in the North

claims.claim: Most of Dany's events could have been reported as hearsay in other viewpoint characters' chapters and been more interesting.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: could have been written as hearsay in other POV characters’ chapters

claims.claim: Ramsay Bolton is a cartoon villain but his victims are very real and the torture is disturbing as it should be.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: Ramsay Bolton is a cartoon villain

claims.claim: Kain quotes and ridicules the New York Times review's opening ('flagons 'n' dragons') while noting it calls Martin 'much better' than Tolkien.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: flagons ’n’ dragons, and swords ’n’ sorcerers

claims.claim: Instead of focusing, book five adds points of view and conflicts, which is exhausting.
claims.source: Alyssa Rosenberg, 'On A Dance With Dragons', ThinkProgress, 15 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: Instead of focusing, the story adds points of view and conflicts

claims.claim: The book gets tangled in a comparative anthropology of sellsword companies.
claims.source: Alyssa Rosenberg, 'On A Dance With Dragons', ThinkProgress, 15 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: a comparative anthropology of sellsword companies. It’s exhausting

claims.claim: The constant punning on 'Reek' is irritating but illustrates how constant the reinforcement must be to brainwash oneself into a new identity.
claims.source: Alyssa Rosenberg, 'On A Dance With Dragons', ThinkProgress, 15 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: The constant punning on Reek

claims.claim: Ramsay is a cartoon psychopath made effective because he is seen from the perspective of the man he has broken.
claims.source: Alyssa Rosenberg, 'On A Dance With Dragons', ThinkProgress, 15 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: a cartoon psychopath, but a genuinely effective one

claims.claim: Theon, Arya and Tyrion all must forget their names and learn new ones, an identity motif binding separate viewpoints.
claims.source: Alyssa Rosenberg, 'On A Dance With Dragons', ThinkProgress, 15 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: have to forget their names and learn new ones

claims.claim: The plotty, cliffhangery reversals (dead! alive! dying! a zombie! in disguise!) are conceded as the selling point.
claims.source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011
claims.quote: the plotty, cliffhangery aspects of Martin’s writing

claims.claim: Doyle parodies the faux-archaic register and unpronounceable invented names in her opening ('yon Good Queen Sady').
claims.source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011
claims.quote: In days of yore, before the Striding Elves sailed West

claims.claim: Arya's plot is a loop of kidnapped/escapes/runs away, and A Clash of Kings is 'The One That Was Really Boring'.
claims.source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011
claims.quote: She gets kidnapped! She escapes! She runs away!

claims.claim: Eastern names are othered against plain Westerosi names like 'Ned', 'Catelyn' and 'Jon'.
claims.source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011
claims.quote: names like “Pyat,” “Xaro Xhoan,” and “Jhogo,”

claims.claim: The essay's core objection is the count of gratuitous rape, molestation and domestic-violence scenes, tallied book by book.
claims.source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011
claims.quote: TWENTY THOUSAND MILLION GRATUITOUS RAPE

claims.claim: The style is unstable, veering from functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms and from an Anglo-Saxon to a Latinate lexicon.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: veers from purely functional modern thriller prose

claims.claim: The default setting of the style is lucid and functional.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: The default setting of Martin’s style is lucid and functional

claims.claim: Martin consistently chooses Anglo-Saxon words over Latinate ones, giving the prose a cumulative woodiness, antiquity and pithiness.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: a cumulative feeling of woodiness, antiquity, pithiness

claims.claim: 'Oft', 'elsewise', 'amongst', 'whilst', 'much and more' and dropped -ly adverbs become annoying pseudo-medieval mannerisms.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: ‘Among’ and ‘while’ become the archaic ‘amongst’ and ‘whilst’

claims.claim: Distorted words ('Ser', girls who have 'flowered') start silly but by sheer repetition come to seem natural.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term

claims.claim: Compounds like sellsword, smallfolk, ironborn, greenseer and weirwood are a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of the style.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of his style

claims.claim: Confrontations are done through terse, charged dialogue that delivers real dramatic shock.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: terse, charged dialogue

claims.claim: Repeated 'cool' and 'still' in the Water Gardens passage may be haste or deliberate torpor-evoking repetition.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: signs of haste, or careful repetitions

claims.claim: Names in three registers (near-familiar, alien, exotic) work on a purely verbal level to pull the reader into a parallel universe.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: the text works on a purely verbal level

claims.claim: The style is uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative

claims.claim: The archaic feel comes from the systematic exclusion of almost all Latin-, Greek- and French-derived words.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013
claims.quote: a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words

claims.claim: Martin uses almost exclusively English prefixes (un-, be-, a-) and native suffixes (-craft, -dom, -ling, -ward).
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013
claims.quote: Martin uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes

claims.claim: Anglo-Saxon compounding lets Martin coin scores of evocative neologisms (archmaester, bannermen, skinchanger, weirwood).
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013
claims.quote: scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms

claims.claim: The result is prose that feels archaic; the medieval sense comes from filtered vocabulary, not stock phrases.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013
claims.quote: The result is to make his prose feel archaic

claims.claim: Martin leans on words he thinks sound archaic and exotic, which in reality sound ridiculous.
claims.source: Asher Gelzer-Govatos, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin', The Erstwhile Philistine, 21 Mar 2012
claims.quote: words that I presume he thinks sound archaic and exotic

claims.claim: 'Jape' for joke is pretentious and a singularly displeasing word.
claims.source: Asher Gelzer-Govatos, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin', The Erstwhile Philistine, 21 Mar 2012
claims.quote: Jape, aside from its pretentiousness, is a singularly displeasing word

claims.claim: 'Mummer's farce' recurs at least ten times in every book.
claims.source: Asher Gelzer-Govatos, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin', The Erstwhile Philistine, 21 Mar 2012
claims.quote: the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book

claims.claim: Giving characters speech patterns (Hodor, Reek's rhymes) is admirable but sometimes inexplicable and tedious across chapters.
claims.source: Asher Gelzer-Govatos, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin', The Erstwhile Philistine, 21 Mar 2012
claims.quote: sometimes his choices are inexplicable

claims.claim: The sex scenes are particularly dire and obviously extraneous.
claims.source: Asher Gelzer-Govatos, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin', The Erstwhile Philistine, 21 Mar 2012
claims.quote: Martin’s scenes are particularly dire

claims.claim: The prose is what holds Martin back from being a truly great author despite strong storytelling.
claims.source: Asher Gelzer-Govatos, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin', The Erstwhile Philistine, 21 Mar 2012
claims.quote: his prose holds him back from being a truly great author

claims.claim: Martin has a knack for vivid, sometimes hallucinogenic description and builds textured scenes of sounds, smells and tastes.
claims.source: Dade Cariaga, 'George RR Martin: American Tolkien?', 19 Sep 2011
claims.quote: textured scenes full of sounds and smells and tastes

claims.claim: For all its vividness the work is pulp with no moral and no depth beneath the diversion.
claims.source: Dade Cariaga, 'George RR Martin: American Tolkien?', 19 Sep 2011
claims.quote: But he writes pulp

claims.claim: Each new wonder carries a strong whiff of making-it-up-as-he-goes.
claims.source: Dade Cariaga, 'George RR Martin: American Tolkien?', 19 Sep 2011
claims.quote: a strong whiff of making-it-up-as-he-goes

claims.claim: Watching the HBO series forgoes the great pleasure of Martin's deft prose.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'A Dance with Dragons: A Masterpiece Worthy of Tolkien', Time, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: the great pleasure of Martin's deft prose

claims.claim: Like Wagner, Martin gives each character recurring leitmotif phrases in their streams of thought ('You know nothing, Jon Snow', 'If I look back I am lost').
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'A Dance with Dragons: A Masterpiece Worthy of Tolkien', Time, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: Like Wagner, he gives each of his characters leitmotifs

claims.claim: Eleven major storylines each have their own rhythm and are written in their own voice, playing off one another.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'A Dance with Dragons: A Masterpiece Worthy of Tolkien', Time, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: each with its own rhythm, written in its own voice

claims.claim: Martin will never win a Pulitzer but his skill as a crafter of narrative exceeds almost any literary novelist's.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'A Dance with Dragons: A Masterpiece Worthy of Tolkien', Time, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: his skill as a crafter of narrative exceeds

claims.claim: After five volumes Martin is a better writer than when he started.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'A Dance with Dragons: A Masterpiece Worthy of Tolkien', Time, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: a better writer than when he started

claims.claim: There is no stock character or cardboard village; every person, wood and street corner has its own tale.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'A Dance with Dragons: A Masterpiece Worthy of Tolkien', Time, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: no such thing as a stock character or a cardboard village

claims.claim: The series is an epic for a more profane, sardonic, ambivalent age than Tolkien's.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'G.R.R. Martin's Complex Epic for an Ambivalent Age', NPR, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: a more profane, more sardonic, more ambivalent age

claims.claim: Tyrion is an actual dwarf, a joke to passers-by, not a hearty axe-wielding fantasy dwarf.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'G.R.R. Martin's Complex Epic for an Ambivalent Age', NPR, 7 Jul 2011
claims.quote: Tyrion is an actual dwarf

claims.claim: Martin is a tense, surging, insomnia-inflicting plotter.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien', Time, 13 Nov 2005
claims.quote: a tense, surging, insomnia-inflicting plotter

claims.claim: Martin is a deft and inexhaustible sketcher of personalities.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien', Time, 13 Nov 2005
claims.quote: a deft and inexhaustible sketcher of personalities

claims.claim: Martin shoots the action from many angles with a dozen narrators to reflect its many-sided nature.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien', Time, 13 Nov 2005
claims.quote: shoots the action from many angles, with a dozen narrators

claims.claim: It is men and women slugging it out in the muck for money, power, lust and love, not elves against orcs.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien', Time, 13 Nov 2005
claims.quote: men and women slugging it out in the muck

claims.claim: Tolkien has imaginative force but one must go elsewhere for moral complexity; Martin's wars are multifaceted and ambiguous.
claims.source: Lev Grossman, 'The American Tolkien', Time, 13 Nov 2005
claims.quote: you have to go elsewhere for moral complexity

claims.claim: Tolkien was never so ponderous nor so obsessed with bodily functions (the Grand Maester befouling himself).
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, 'A Dance with Dragons', 26 Sep 2011
claims.quote: Tolkien was never quite so ponderous

claims.claim: Book five is cynical, dark, with few laughs and not much action, mostly exposition.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, 'A Dance with Dragons', 26 Sep 2011
claims.quote: a little cynical, plenty dark, with not many laughs

claims.claim: Jon Snow's chapters go 'all Hamlety', soliciting input and keeping his own counsel.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, 'A Dance with Dragons', 26 Sep 2011
claims.quote: comes over all Hamlety, wondering what to do

claims.claim: On the evidence one wonders whether Martin is getting tired of the series.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, 'A Dance with Dragons', 26 Sep 2011
claims.quote: one wonders if Martin isn’t getting a little tired

claims.claim: The series is told through an array of constantly shifting perspectives across many locales.
claims.source: Bill Sheehan, 'A Dance with Dragons worth the long long wait', Washington Post, 12 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: an array of constantly shifting perspectives

claims.claim: Vividly rendered set pieces, cliffhangers and appalling cruelty make it epic fantasy as it should be written.
claims.source: Bill Sheehan, 'A Dance with Dragons worth the long long wait', Washington Post, 12 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: passionate, compelling, convincingly detailed and thoroughly imagined

claims.claim: The book feels grounded in brutal medieval reality, closer to the Wars of the Roses than to Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Bill Sheehan, 'A Dance with Dragons worth the long long wait', Washington Post, 12 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: grounded in the brutal reality of medieval times

claims.claim: Characters repeatedly remind the reader that 'Winter is coming'.
claims.source: Bill Sheehan, 'A Dance with Dragons worth the long long wait', Washington Post, 12 Jul 2011 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: as the characters repeatedly remind us

claims.claim: Martin writes as convincingly of tart apple juice as of mountain sleet; the book is an adventure of the senses.
claims.source: Paul Levinson, review of A Game of Thrones, Tangent #16, Fall 1996 (author's 2011 repost)
claims.quote: tart juices oozing from an apple as of sleet

claims.claim: The descriptive passages are marvellous; you can smell the spice and taste every cup of wine.
claims.source: Paul Levinson, review of A Game of Thrones, Tangent #16, Fall 1996 (author's 2011 repost)
claims.quote: you can smell the spice

claims.claim: The 1996 trade review credits superbly developed characters and accomplished prose.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, review of A Game of Thrones, 29 Jul 1996
claims.quote: superbly developed characters, accomplished prose

claims.claim: Across four books there is no development, progression or climax; the plot is like banging unrelated chords on a piano.
claims.source: Matt Hilliard, 'A Song of Ice and Fire 1–4', Yet There Are Statues, 14 Aug 2010
claims.quote: banging an endless series of chords

claims.claim: Martin's world is a social landscape built from people rather than physical description.
claims.source: Matt Hilliard, 'A Song of Ice and Fire 1–4', Yet There Are Statues, 14 Aug 2010
claims.quote: he has constructed a social landscape

claims.claim: The series' approach emphasised intrigue and realism over magic and elevated prose.
claims.source: Matt Hilliard, 'A Song of Ice and Fire 1–4', Yet There Are Statues, 14 Aug 2010
claims.quote: intrigue and realism over magic and elevated prose

claims.claim: Naming each chapter for its viewpoint character solves the confusion that shifting POV can cause.
claims.source: Shannon Roberts, 'Reviewing A Game of Thrones: a first-50 review', The Editorial Department (20th-anniversary piece; page stamped 2024-01-07)
claims.quote: a clearly titled chapter solves the problem admirably

claims.claim: A swift pace and plenty of action introduce three conflicts within the first fifty pages.
claims.source: Shannon Roberts, 'Reviewing A Game of Thrones: a first-50 review', The Editorial Department (20th-anniversary piece; page stamped 2024-01-07)
claims.quote: a swift pace and plenty of action

claims.claim: Keeping magic to small, measured doses maintains suspense.
claims.source: Shannon Roberts, 'Reviewing A Game of Thrones: a first-50 review', The Editorial Department (20th-anniversary piece; page stamped 2024-01-07)
claims.quote: keeping the magic to small, measured doses

claims.claim: Individual chapters are good enough to stand as award-worthy short stories.
claims.source: Thomas M. Wagner, SFF180 review of A Dance with Dragons (undated, c. 2011)
claims.quote: good enough to function on their own as award-worthy short stories

claims.claim: Martin writes chapters out of order and sequences them later, like a film editor.
claims.source: Thomas M. Wagner, SFF180 review of A Dance with Dragons (undated, c. 2011)
claims.quote: he writes chapters out of order, and then sequences them later

claims.claim: The writing never falls below the highest standards of literary craft.
claims.source: Thomas M. Wagner, SFF180 review of A Dance with Dragons (undated, c. 2011)
claims.quote: the highest standards of literary craft

claims.claim: Martin's uncanny prose style contains a detailed realism that brings Tyrion to life on the page.
claims.source: Nicholas Pompella, '25 Years On, a Mixed Legacy for A Game of Thrones', National Review, 7 Aug 2021 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: Martin’s uncanny prose style contains a detailed realism

claims.feature: politics to the exclusion of all else
claims.claim: The book is coarsely obsessed with politics to the exclusion of almost everything but sex and violence.
claims.source: Nicholas Pompella, '25 Years On, a Mixed Legacy for A Game of Thrones', National Review, 7 Aug 2021 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: coarsely obsessed with politics

claims.claim: The fantasy trappings dress a bloated Agatha Christie whodunit plotline that goes nowhere.
claims.source: Nicholas Pompella, '25 Years On, a Mixed Legacy for A Game of Thrones', National Review, 7 Aug 2021 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: a type of bloated Agatha Christie plotline

claims.claim: The book becomes predictable once the reader reads every event through cynical Machiavellianism.
claims.source: Nicholas Pompella, '25 Years On, a Mixed Legacy for A Game of Thrones', National Review, 7 Aug 2021 (read via Wayback)
claims.quote: the book becomes predictable as the reader grows accustomed

claims.claim: Adam Roberts's Fantasy: A Short History says Martin lets readers have their chivalric cake and eat it too, thrilling at poisonings, rapes and betrayals while enamoured of noble houses and titles; no sentence-level prose judgment is reported.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt reviewing Adam Roberts, Fantasy: A Short History, Strange Horizons, 2026 (Roberts's judgments as quoted by Burt)
claims.quote: have their chivalric cake and eat it too

claims.claim: The Washington Post's 1996 review faulted one-dimensional characters and less than memorable imagery.
claims.source: Bookmarks Reviews roundup of 1996 reviews of A Game of Thrones (quoting John H. Riskind, Washington Post, 28 Jul 1996)
claims.quote: one-dimensional characters and less than memorable imagery

claims.claim: Dana Jennings's Times review says the book, like all proper serials, gives no emotional respite and ends on razor-sharp question marks.
claims.source: BookBrowse review roundup for A Dance with Dragons (quoting Dana Jennings, New York Times, Jul 2011), read via Wayback
claims.quote: ending with several razor-sharp question marks

claims.claim: Martin's writing is well above average for commercial prose, but he is not a seven-drafts literary reviser.
claims.source: Michael O. Church, 'The Tragedy of George R. R. Martin', Substack, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: well above average for commercial prose
